title: In the Blink of an Eye: A Perspective on Film Editing (2nd ed.)
key_findings: Rule of Six for choosing a cut, ranked with weights: emotion 51%, story 23%, rhythm 10%, eye-trace 7%, 2D plane of screen 5%, 3D space of action 4% (weights as reported by several secondary summaries: StudioBinder, NoFilmSchool, PremiumBeat).
Ranking rule: if something must be given up, give up from the bottom (3D space) before the top (emotion).
The blink as punctuation of thought is a separate idea in the book, not one of the six criteria (secondary summaries).
practical_applications: Ask 'is this cut true to the emotion of the moment' before checking continuity details.
When an AI shot has a continuity flaw but the right emotion, keep it.
limitations: Practitioner judgement, not an experiment; the percentages are rhetorical, not measured.
Book itself not read this session; content from publisher page and secondary summaries.

title: Film Art: An Introduction (many editions since 1979; 12th ed. translated into Russian 2024)
authors: David Bordwell, Kristin Thompson, Jeff Smith
key_findings: Standard university textbook for film form and style (mise-en-scene, cinematography, editing, sound, genre); described as 'the gold standard for humanistic introductory film analysis pedagogy' by Ignashev & Rybina (2025), the article used here to confirm the edition history.
practical_applications: Terminology base for continuity editing, 180-degree system, eyeline match, shot/reverse shot used in FD10/FD11.
limitations: Textbook content not read this session; existence and status confirmed via a 2025 article abstract (OpenAlex).

title: Intensified Continuity: Visual Style in Contemporary American Film
key_findings: Film Quarterly 55(3):16-28. Contemporary Hollywood style intensifies rather than abandons classical continuity.
Between 1930 and 1960 most Hollywood features had 300-700 shots, ASL about 8-11 s; later many films measured at 3-6 s (search snippets).

Names four tactics of camerawork/editing as central (rapid editing, bipolar lens lengths, close framings in dialogue, free-ranging camera are the commonly cited four; exact wording not confirmed in snippets).
practical_applications: Short-form vertical video inherits intensified continuity: fast cutting but still continuity logic.
limitations: Full text not read; only search snippets and bibliographic records.

title: Intensified continuity revisited (blog essay)
key_findings: Compares The Shop Around the Corner (Lubitsch, 1940) with its remake You've Got Mail: outdoor section 2 shots (~82 s each) vs 41 shots (~4.1 s); cafe section 14 shots (~21 s) vs 84 shots (~4.3 s); running times nearly equal.

Intensified continuity: rapid cutting, dialogue broken into OTS and singles, tight shot/reverse shot, reaction and POV shots replacing sustained staging, redundant coverage, more demonstrative acting, more non-diegetic music, long takes kept for virtuoso travelling shots.
It is an intensification of, not a break from, continuity principles; praises Zodiac (Fincher) as intelligent use.
practical_applications: Use the comparison as a test: same scene staged in 2 long takes vs cut into many singles; compare what the audience feels.
limitations: Expert blog by a film scholar, not peer reviewed; ASL from his own counts.

title: The Attentional Theory of Cinematic Continuity
key_findings: AToCC: continuity is perceived when attention is cued across the cut by natural cues (off-screen sounds, conversational turns, motion onsets, gaze cues, pointing, exits from frame, rhythmic patterns); viewers need not build a coherent 3D model of the space.

If expectations (screen location, orientation, direction of action) are met within a few frames after the cut, continuity is 'a priori'; if not, the viewer enters effortful 'a posteriori' reconstruction and becomes aware of the construction.
Match-action: Blade Runner (1982) cut puts Rachael's face where Deckard's was; whip pan in Dancer in the Dark (2000) causes uncoordinated gaze/OKR eye movements that may feel like seasickness.

Shot/reverse shot: viewers keep 'attentional pointers' to where each character is on screen; about 200 ms after an off-screen speaker starts, attention shifts to their previous screen location. Requiem for a Dream (2000) example crosses the line and mismatches eyelines.
Last Year in Marienbad (1961) and Melies show match-action can hide impossible changes.
Credits Block's The Visual Story (2001) for tracking centres of interest across cuts.
practical_applications: Before each cut, name the cue that moves the eye (look, sound, motion) and place the target where the eye will land.
For AI shots that do not match, cut on motion and keep screen position of the face.
limitations: Theory with illustrative eye-tracking demos, not a single controlled test of every rule.

title: Edit Blindness: The relationship between attention and global change blindness in dynamic scenes
authors: Tim J. Smith, John M. Henderson
key_findings: Participants told to detect edits in feature-film excerpts still missed many; edits following continuity rules produced more edit blindness.
About a quarter of edits joining two viewpoints of the same scene were undetected; about a third when the edit coincided with sudden motion onset.
A few misses are due to blinks/saccades, but most are due to inattention.
practical_applications: Cut on motion onset to hide joins between generated shots.
limitations: Detection task differs from normal viewing; feature-film clips, not vertical short video.

title: Attentional synchrony and the influence of viewing task on gaze behavior in static and dynamic scenes
authors: Tim J. Smith, Parag K. Mital
key_findings: Free viewing of dynamic scenes produced more attentional synchrony, longer fixations and more gaze to people and high-flicker areas than static scenes.
A task (spot-the-location) reduced synchrony and moved gaze away from people and flicker, but endogenous control is slow to start: first saccades default to screen centre and motion.
practical_applications: In the first second, put the subject near centre and give it the motion; viewers' task (scrolling to decide) still starts from centre/motion.
limitations: Unedited real-world videos, not narrative films.

title: Clustering of Gaze During Dynamic Scene Viewing is Predicted by Motion
authors: Parag K. Mital, Tim J. Smith, Robin L. Hill, John M. Henderson
key_findings: Temporal features (flicker, motion and their contrasts) were the most predictive of where viewers look in dynamic scenes; mid-level static features less so (Semantic Scholar TLDR).
practical_applications: The moving thing wins attention; keep background motion lower than subject motion.
limitations: Only TLDR read.

title: What Would Jaws Do? The Tyranny of Film and the Relationship between Gaze and Higher-Level Narrative Film Comprehension
authors: Lester C. Loschky, Adam M. Larson, Joseph P. Magliano, Tim J. Smith
key_findings: 12-s Moonraker clip; Context group (saw prior 2.5 min) drew the critical inference more (91% vs 71%).

Both groups showed strong attentional synchrony vs shuffled baseline (d > 2.98); comprehension differences in gaze were small (d about 0.42, p = .054). The film-driven effect was estimated 1.5-6x larger than the mental-model effect ('tyranny of film').
practical_applications: Editing can steer where people look regardless of what they understand; understanding must come from story information, not from gaze control alone.
limitations: Single clip (follow-up with another film similar), few fixations per participant.

title: The Scene Perception & Event Comprehension Theory (SPECT) Applied to Visual Narratives
authors: Lester C. Loschky, Adam M. Larson, Tim J. Smith, Joseph P. Magliano
key_findings: Front-end processes (within a fixation: attentional selection, information extraction) vs back-end processes (across fixations: building event models in working memory and episodic memory).
Applies to picture stories, comics and film; medium-specific differences in front-end processing.
practical_applications: Shot design serves front-end (where to look, what to extract); sequence design serves back-end (what is happening, what will happen).
limitations: Theory paper; abstract only read.

title: Neurocinematics: The Neuroscience of Film
authors: Uri Hasson, Ohad Landesman, Barbara Knappmeyer, Ignacio Vallines, Nava Rubin, David J. Heeger
key_findings: Inter-subject correlation (ISC) of fMRI: Alfred Hitchcock Presents 'Bang! You're Dead' (1961) >65% of cortex; The Good, the Bad and the Ugly (1966) 45%; Curb Your Enthusiasm (2000) 18%; unedited one-shot Washington Square Park video <5%.
Eye-position also more consistent for the structured film than the one-shot reality video.
ISC over time rose near the Hitchcock climax; auditory cortex ISC high throughout (0.67).
Authors note Curb is often shot without a script; sample was college students.
practical_applications: Directed structure (framing, cutting, sound) makes audiences respond alike; an unedited static shot lets attention scatter.
limitations: Small samples; 'control' is not the same as quality or enjoyment (critiqued by Poulaki 2014).

title: Synchronization of spontaneous eyeblinks while viewing video stories
authors: Tamami Nakano, Yoshiharu Yamamoto, Keiichi Kitajo, Toshimitsu Takahashi, Shigeru Kitazawa
key_findings: Blinks were synchronised within and between viewers of the same video stories, but not tied to scene breaks.
Synchronised blinks occurred at moments needing less attention: end of an action, absence of the main character, long shots, repeated similar scenes.
No synchronisation for background video or audio-only story.
practical_applications: Murch's intuition that cuts land at 'blink points' fits: people blink at the end of an action - a natural cut point.
limitations: Short Mr Bean-style videos; does not test edits directly.
license: CC BY (Proc R Soc B open access)

title: Attention and the Evolution of Hollywood Film
authors: James E. Cutting, Jordan E. DeLong, Christine E. Nothelfer
key_findings: 150 films 1935-2005: shot lengths became more correlated with neighbours and power spectra approached 1/f.
Authors suggest 1/f shot structure may help harness attention.
practical_applications: Group shots of similar length into runs (calm run, fast run) rather than random alternation.
limitations: Correlational; the attention claim is the authors' suggestion.

title: Quicker, Faster, Darker: Changes in Hollywood Film over 75 Years
authors: James E. Cutting, Kaitlin L. Brunick, Jordan E. DeLong, Catalina Iricinschi, Ayse Candan
key_findings: 160 films 1935-2010: shorter shots, more motion, shorter shots carry proportionately more motion in recent films, and films got darker.
Authors suggest all four trends reflect filmmakers trying to control attention more.
practical_applications: Pair short shots with more motion; long shots with stillness.
limitations: English-language popular films only; correlational.

title: Shot Durations, Shot Classes, and the Increased Pace of Popular Movies
key_findings: 9,400 English and 1,550 non-English movies 1912-2013: mean shot duration declines roughly linearly on a log scale in the sound era.
In 24 films 1940-2010 the decline is uniform across 15 shot classes; 25% of decline from shift toward shot classes that are shorter; 8% from larger (closer) shot scales.
Explores proportions of shot classes across genres.
practical_applications: Closer shots tend to be shorter; cutting pace and shot scale move together.
limitations: Abstract only; genre-specific numbers not read.

title: The evolution of pace in popular movies
key_findings: Across four roughly equal acts (setup, complication, development, climax): shot durations increase and motion decreases in the setup; images darken across complication/development and brighten across the climax; shots shorten and motion rises in the first part of the climax, then lengthen with less motion at the end.
Brighter/darker images are associated with positive/negative emotion (author's interpretation).
practical_applications: Shape a clip's pace curve: calm open, darken in the middle, fastest cutting at the climax start, slow out at the end.
limitations: Feature-length English-language films; mapping to 15-60 s clips is an inference.

title: The Kuleshov Effect: Recreating the Classic Experiment
key_findings: Cinema Journal 31(2):59-75. Recreated Kuleshov's design (neutral face - emotional image - neutral face, checklist rating); most participants chose 'no emotion' - no Kuleshov effect found (as summarised by Calbi et al. 2017 and Wikipedia).
practical_applications: Do not rely on context alone to put emotion on a blank face.
limitations: Single trial per condition, low statistical power (critique by later authors). Paper itself not read.

title: The Kuleshov Effect: the influence of contextual framing on emotional attributions
authors: Dean Mobbs, Nikolaus Weiskopf, Hakwan C. Lau, Eric Featherstone, Ray J. Dolan, Chris D. Frith
key_findings: n = 14 in fMRI; identical faces paired with neutral vs emotional movies changed ratings of expression and mental state.
Emotional context enhanced responses in temporal pole, ACC, amygdala, STS; amygdala interaction for subtle happy/fear faces with congruent context.
practical_applications: Subtle faces + strong context = the context-driven reading works best when the face is ambiguous, not blank.
limitations: Small n; departs from the classic paradigm (faces were subtle, not strictly neutral, per Calbi 2017).

title: Does the Kuleshov Effect Really Exist? Revisiting a Classic Film Experiment on Facial Expressions and Emotional Contexts
authors: Daniel Barratt, Anna Cabak Redei, Ase Innes-Ker, Joost van de Weijer
key_findings: Published in Perception. 36 participants, 24 film sequences of neutral faces, six emotional conditions, eye tracking.

'Some sort of Kuleshov effect does in fact exist': participants chose the congruent category more often than alternatives; valence and arousal in expected directions (sad context = most negative/least arousing; desire context = most positive/most arousing, per Calbi 2017).
practical_applications: Context cuts shift emotion reading; the effect is a nudge, not a rewrite.
limitations: Moderate sample; effect sizes modest; abstract only read.

title: How Context Influences Our Perception of Emotional Faces: A Behavioral Study on the Kuleshov Effect
authors: Marta Calbi, Katrin Heimann, Daniel Barratt, Francesca Siri, Maria A. Umilta, Vittorio Gallese
key_findings: 28 adults; face (1.5 s) - dynamic context (3 s) - face (1.5 s).
Fearful context made neutral faces more negative and more arousing; happy context had no significant effect on valence/arousal; categorisation followed context.
Reviews earlier replications: Prince & Hensley null (low power), Mobbs positive, Barratt positive.
practical_applications: Fear/threat context is the most reliable Kuleshov lever; happy context is weaker.
limitations: Small n, two emotions, grayscale, no sound; text/table inconsistency in neutral condition.

title: Do not cross the line: Heuristic spatial updating in dynamic scenes
key_findings: Two-shot clips of cars: when ambiguous, viewers judged 'same direction' if cars shared screen direction (left-right heuristic).
When environmental cues conflicted with screen direction, reaction times were longer: viewers use a screen-direction heuristic, switching to effortful alignment when cues are incongruent.
practical_applications: Keep screen direction constant for the same journey; if you must flip it, give a clear environmental cue and accept a comprehension cost.
limitations: Simple car stimuli; abstract only.

title: The influence of camera angle on comprehension and retention of pictorial events
key_findings: Camera angle had significant, predictable effects on judgments of characters' physical and personal characteristics and on recall of story gist (Semantic Scholar TLDR).
practical_applications: Angle changes how a character is judged; use it deliberately.
limitations: Still-picture sequences; only TLDR read; direction and size of effects not checked here.

title: Perceiving the Language of Films
key_findings: Children aged 7, 9 and 13 watched a four-shot action sequence edited two ways and reconstructed the action from pictures of the shots (TLDR); cited by Smith 2012 as evidence viewers can comprehend spatial layout of edited sequences.
practical_applications: Film grammar is learned; very young or inexperienced viewers need clearer establishing information.
limitations: TLDR only; results detail not read.

title: 'Cuts in Action': A High-Density EEG Study Investigating the Neural Correlates of Different Editing Techniques in Film
authors: Katrin S. Heimann, Sebo Uithol, Marta Calbi, Maria A. Umilta, Michele Guerra, Vittorio Gallese
key_findings: Cuts in general elicit early ERP components resembling syntactic-violation responses (as in language/music).

Continuity edits and cuts across the 180-degree line differ in later components (spatial remapping, awareness); occipital alpha did not support a pure attention account; central mu-rhythm (sensorimotor) differences found.
practical_applications: Crossing the line is processed differently even when not consciously noticed - use it on purpose (disorientation), not by accident.
limitations: Lab EEG with short action clips; abstract only.

title: Moving Mirrors: A High-density EEG Study Investigating the Effect of Camera Movements on Motor Cortex Activation during Action Observation
authors: Katrin Heimann, Maria A. Umilta, Michele Guerra, Vittorio Gallese
key_findings: Same hand action filmed fixed, zoom-in, dolly-in, Steadicam-in: Steadicam approach produced the strongest mu-rhythm desynchronisation.
Ratings: approaching camera felt more involving; Steadicam felt closest to a human approaching.
practical_applications: For involvement/intimacy, a gentle physical push-in (with slight human float) beats an optical zoom.
limitations: Hand actions only; lab setting.

title: Watching More Closely: Shot Scale Affects Film Viewers' Theory of Mind Tendency But Not Ability
key_findings: N = 136; sad close-up of a character led to more spontaneous mental-state references to her than long shot (b = 0.104, p = .05) or neutral close-up (b = 0.128, p = .013), mainly affective references.
No transfer to the other character; no change in prompted ToM ability.
practical_applications: Close-up works with an expressive face: the close-up amplifies what the face carries, it does not create it.
limitations: One 2-min animated film, young convenience sample, single coder.

title: Shot scale matters: The effect of close-up frequency on mental state attribution in film viewers
authors: Katalin E. Balint, Janine N. Blessing, Brendan Rooney
key_findings: Online N = 495; 13 versions of an animated film varying number of facial close-ups (0 to several) x 2 facial expressions; measured spontaneous and prompted mental-state attribution in story retellings.
practical_applications: Close-up frequency is a dial for how much viewers think about a character's mind.
limitations: Abstract read only; detailed dose-response result not read here.

title: A century of Gestalt psychology in visual perception: I. Perceptual grouping and figure-ground organization
authors: Johan Wagemans, James H. Elder, Michael Kubovy, Stephen E. Palmer, Mary A. Peterson, Manish Singh, Rudiger von der Heydt
key_findings: Gestalt psychology started with Wertheimer's 1912 paper on phi (apparent) motion.
Grouping principles: proximity, similarity, common fate, good continuation, closure, symmetry, parallelism; newer: synchrony, common region, element and uniform connectedness.
Figure-ground is influenced by past experience and attention.
practical_applications: Common fate and synchrony in motion: things moving together read as one group; use for crowds, product + hand, kinetic type.
limitations: Review of static and dynamic grouping; film-specific tests not covered.

title: The Visual Story: Creating the Visual Structure of Film, TV, and Digital Media (3rd ed.)
key_findings: Seven basic visual components: space, line, shape, tone, colour, movement, rhythm.
Principle of Contrast & Affinity applies to all components: more contrast = more visual intensity; affinity = less.
Links visual structure to story structure (intensity curve). 1st ed. Focal Press 2001.
practical_applications: Plot a visual-intensity graph next to the story-intensity graph and make them rise together.
limitations: Practitioner craft; book not read beyond publisher/TOC pages.

title: Visual Narrative Structure
key_findings: Narrative Grammar for sequential images: narrative categories (e.g. establisher, initial, peak, release) in a canonical arc that can embed recursively; pacing reflects embedding patterns.
Theory proposed to extend to film.
practical_applications: Carousels and storyboards: give each panel a role (establish, initiate, peak, release).
limitations: Comics-based theory; film application is proposed, abstract only.

title: A Semantic/Syntactic Approach to Film Genre
key_findings: Cinema Journal 23(3):6-18. Genre can be defined semantically (a list of elements: settings, props, character types) or syntactically (the structural relations between them); the two are complementary.
practical_applications: A genre look is not only props and lighting (semantics) but the relationship pattern (syntax): who threatens whom, what is withheld.
limitations: Read via summaries and bibliographic database, not full text.

title: Towards a Semiotics of Film Lighting
key_findings: Summarises Place & Peterson's 'Some Visual Motifs of Film Noir' (1976): uses Hollywood technical terms - key/fill/back light, low key (high contrast) vs high key (low contrast), spotted vs flooded light, high vs low light direction, highlight and shadow modelling - to describe noir style.
practical_applications: Describe a genre's light with technical terms (key/fill ratio, direction, spot vs flood) when prompting AI.
limitations: Only the opening excerpt (OpenAlex abstract) read.

title: Hitchcock and Narrative Suspense: Theory and Practice
key_findings: Discusses Noel Carroll's theory: suspense arises when a desirable (moral) outcome is unlikely and an undesirable outcome is likely; example D.W. Griffith's The Lonely Villa (1909) with cross-cutting between the threatened heroine and the distant hero.
practical_applications: Cross-cutting creates suspense only if the audience knows the stakes and the odds.
limitations: Abstract/excerpt only.

title: Acting in the Cinema
key_findings: University of California Press; chapters on protocols, rhetoric and expressive technique, 'Expressive Coherence and Performance within Performance', star case studies, Rear Window and The King of Comedy as performance texts (TOC only).
practical_applications: Vocabulary for screen performance analysis.
limitations: Only catalogue/TOC confirmed; argument not read.

title: Effects of 'In-Your-Face' Television Discourse on Perceptions of a Legitimate Opposition
key_findings: Experiments: televised discourse raises awareness of opposing views, but incivility and close-up camera perspectives made audiences see opposing views as less legitimate.
practical_applications: Close-ups on conflict intensify negative reactions to the person shown - a proxemic 'too close' effect; for a trusted expert, avoid aggressive ECU during disagreement.
limitations: Political TV debates, US sample; abstract only.

title: Moment-to-Moment Optimal Branding in TV Commercials: Preventing Avoidance by Pulsing
authors: Thales S. Teixeira, Michel Wedel, Rik Pieters
key_findings: Eye tracking on 31 commercials, nearly 2,000 participants, zapping data: attention dispersion strongly predicts avoidance.
Central on-screen brand positions (not brand size) promote avoidance; brand 'pulsing' (short repeated appearances, same total exposure) reduces avoidance - confirmed with edited commercials.
practical_applications: Do not park a big logo centre-frame at the start; pulse the brand in short touches.
limitations: TV ads with zapping, pre-feed era; transfer to swipe feeds is an inference.

title: Emotion-Induced Engagement in Internet Video Advertisements
authors: Thales S. Teixeira, Michel Wedel, Rik Pieters
key_findings: Facial-expression detection (joy, surprise), eye tracking and zapping: surprise and joy concentrate attention and retain viewers.

The level of surprise matters most for attention concentration; the velocity (rate of increase) of joy matters most for retention; joy effect asymmetric (gains for increases larger than losses for decreases).
practical_applications: Build joy upward in steps; place surprise early to concentrate gaze.
limitations: Internet ads circa 2010; lab setting.

title: Measure key moments for audience retention (YouTube Help)
key_findings: Intro = % of audience still watching after the first 30 seconds; flat line = watched start to finish; gradual decline typical; spikes = rewatching/sharing (or confusion); dips = abandoning/skipping.
Advice: align title/thumbnail with content, experiment with the first 30 s, move compelling content earlier.
practical_applications: Read retention graphs after posting; mark dips against the edit timeline.
limitations: Long-form videos; platform docs change over time.

title: Understand your YouTube content performance (YouTube Help)
key_findings: 'Stayed to watch' = percentage of times viewers stayed to watch past the initial seconds of a Short; engaged views exclude loops; average view duration computed from engaged views.
No Shorts-specific retention advice or benchmarks on this page.
practical_applications: For Shorts, the first seconds decide 'stayed to watch'; measure that before anything else.
limitations: Page does not state how many seconds 'initial seconds' is.

title: Creative best practices for performance ads (TikTok Ads Help)
key_findings: Prioritise the hook in the first 6 seconds; introduce the content proposition in the first 3 seconds.
Use sound/music; captions/text 5-10 words per second; 9:16, at least 720p; keep content in the UI safe zone.
Structure hook -> USPs -> CTA; use transitions, stickers, graphics to retain view time; 3-5 creatives per ad group.
practical_applications: Vertical promo template: 0-3 s proposition, by 6 s the hook landed, then proof, then CTA.
limitations: Ad-performance guidance from the platform; no published evidence base.

title: Cinemetrics, Part of the Humanities' Cyberinfrastructure
key_findings: Cinemetrics (cinemetrics.lv) is an open-access site that collects and processes scholarly data on film editing, primarily cutting rates (shot lengths).
practical_applications: Measure ASL of a reference film/clip before imitating its pace.
limitations: Crowd-submitted measurements vary in accuracy.

title: Neurocinematics and the discourse of control: Towards a critical neurofilmology
key_findings: Critiques Hasson et al.'s use of 'control' (predictable activation by film stimuli) as resting on a unidirectional model of communication that brackets out 'noisy' divergent viewers; argues those cases matter for a complex view of film-mind interaction.
practical_applications: Do not equate high inter-subject correlation with quality or liking.
limitations: Theoretical critique; abstract only.
